title: General scales unlock AI evaluation with explanatory and predictive power
explain_beginner: Today's AI tests usually give one score, which tells you little about what a system can really do or how it will handle something new. This paper introduces broad scales that describe two things: what a task demands and what abilities an AI system has. Using 18 rubrics, the authors placed 15 language models across 63 tasks on these scales. The result explains what familiar benchmarks actually measure and predicts performance on new tasks better than strong baseline methods. This matters because it gives a clearer, more reliable picture of AI strengths and limits, which supports safer deployment and better audits.
explain_business: Most AI evaluations today reduce a system to a single score from a benchmark, which is hard to use when deciding whether to deploy it on a new task. This paper offers broad scales that profile what a task demands and what an AI system can do. The authors show these profiles predict performance on new tasks and benchmarks better than strong baseline predictors. In practice, this means audits and procurement decisions can rely on evidence that explains and predicts rather than one headline number. It informs decisions about where to trust an AI system, where its limits lie, and how to compare options before committing to deployment.
explain_practitioner: The authors propose broad scales for AI evaluation, built from 18 rubrics covering a wide range of mental and intellectual demands. These scales place different task instances on a common footing, producing profiles of what benchmarks actually measure and profiles of a system's general strengths and limits. The method is fully automated and was demonstrated on 15 large language models across 63 tasks. Key results include validity evidence from how sensitive and specific benchmarks are, an explanation for conflicting claims about AI reasoning, and predictions at the level of individual task instances that beat strong opaque baselines, especially on unfamiliar tasks and benchmarks.
